title: Q&A: What Has Emerged From the Trial of a Businessman Charged in the Murder of a Maltese Journalist?
content:
OCCRP: Daphne Caruana Galizia is said to have coined a phrase that has been picked up by anti-corruption activists: “Malta is not a normal country." Are there any aspects of this trial that bring the phrase to mind now that the lawyers have made their final arguments, and the jury will soon reach its verdict?

Julian Bonnici: The political shadow over the case is a long one. Keith Schembri, the former chief of staff to Malta's ex-prime minister spent close to four days in the witness box, and has been accused throughout the trial of being the real mastermind. He denies it, and little hard evidence for it has been put before the jury.

The trial has also laid out defendant Yorgen Fenech's web of contacts across Malta's political elite: his WhatsApp exchanges with Schembri, with former Prime Minister Joseph Muscat, with regulatory heads, and with the deputy police commissioner who once headed the investigation into the murder.

A lot of people know that Caruana Galizia was Malta’s most prominent investigative journalist and anti-corruption activist. Who is Yorgen Fenech, and what is the prosecution alleging motivated him to commission her murder?

title: A Key Food Source Collapsed Off West Africa’s Coast as Chinese Ships Ground the Species Into Fishmeal
content:
As the day draws to a close in Bubaque, a remote island in Guinea-Bissau, fishermen are arriving with their day’s catch, pulling canoes onto a muddy bank teeming with crabs.

It’s a common scene here in the Bijagós Archipelago, and elsewhere along the West African coast. And one species is especially prized as a source of high-quality protein — the sardinella.

But the small and silvery fish has been decimated in Guinea-Bissau’s coastal waters, according to an internal fisheries assessment produced for the government and obtained by OCCRP.

The assessment was carried out in 2025 by the Atlantic branch of the Russian Federal Research Institute of Fisheries and Oceanography (VNIRO), which worked with scientists from INIPO, Guinea-Bissau’s oceanographic institute. 

While the assessment does not delve into the cause of the decline, a government official attributed it to the recent rise of the local fishmeal industry, which grinds up large volumes of the sardinella and other fish to make a nutrient-dense powder that is fed to farm animals around the world.

title: FAQ: What to Know About Ireland’s Probe Into Our Reporting on Its Alumina Exports to Russia
content:
After OCCRP and partners published an investigation in March exposing how Europe’s largest alumina refinery was feeding into a supply chain linked to Russian weapons manufacturers, the reaction was big. 

Lawmakers and officials across Europe called for Brussels to halt all exports of alumina — the key input needed to produce aluminum — to Russia, in hopes of dealing another blow to Putin’s war machine. 

In Ireland, where the factory is based, the government promised to investigate the matter, and announced late last month that it had shared the findings of its probe with the European Commission. 

The report has not been made public, but The Irish Times obtained a leaked copy and shared it with OCCRP and other media partners. 

Here is what the leaked report says, what remains unknown, and what could come next. 

As a key resource for industries ranging from energy to defense, the powdery precursor to aluminum known as alumina has been branded a “critical raw material” by the European Union, whose leaders have called on member states to stockpile the good as a bulwark against hostile powers.

title: Albania's Cheerful 'AI Minister' Is the Product of a Government Agency Under Investigation for Massive Corruption
content:
Last September, Albania made headlines around the world when it introduced the world’s first-ever “AI minister.”

Diella, which means “Sun” in Albanian, was a chatbot that had been promoted to ministerial status. Her remit, Prime Minister Edi Rama announced, was to ensure that “public tenders will be 100 percent free of corruption.”

“I do not have personal ambitions or interests,” the AI avatar, who dresses in traditional costume, told parliament in her maiden speech. “I only have data, a thirst for knowledge, and algorithms dedicated to serving citizens… free from prejudice, discrimination, clientelism, nepotism, or corruption.” 

At the time, there were doubts over whether Diella could offer any real solution to Albania’s long-standing corruption problem. 

It appears that some of the reservations may have been well-founded. Experts caution that Albania’s plan to use Diella as a buffer against corruption has flaws, given that information generated by AI is not inherently neutral, and that there has been little transparency so far on how the technology will be deployed.

title: From Headlines to Impact: Connecting Journalism and Civil Society to Drive Accountability in Ukraine
content:
Navigating the intersecting frontlines of a brutal war and structural state reforms, OCCRP and a network of Ukrainian partners have introduced a new approach for driving reform and accountability in the country. 

Established in 2025, this collaborative framework aims to advance deep-dive investigative journalism and connect those findings to the policy efforts of leading advocacy groups. By linking high-impact reporting with civil society expertise, the partners work to expose wrongdoing, trigger concrete legal action, close regulatory loopholes, and tighten international sanctions.

While OCCRP’s editorial teams support the work of Ukrainian media partners, the Impact Department coordinates with a network of civil society organizations and the accountability ecosystem. This approach maximizes their complementary strengths while strictly preserving their independence. It draws inspiration from the decade-old Global Anti-Corruption Consortium — a partnership between OCCRP and Transparency International that an external evaluation found to be five times more effective than traditional reporting alone.

title: The Rise and Fall of Kyrgyzstan’s Seemingly Untouchable Security Chief
content:
In a room decorated with colorful balloons and wall murals, a group of Kyrgyz children pose for the camera.

The boys, seated in front, wear traditional kalpak hats and clutch boxed building sets. Behind them, girls wearing yellow dresses and matching bows hold oversized plush dolls.

The children, celebrating the opening of their new kindergarten, are joined by an unusual guest: Standing behind them is a stern-looking man wearing a dark-blue suit and an inscrutable expression. This is Kamchybek Tashiev, at the time the head of Kyrgyzstan’s feared GKNB security service.

Under his leadership, the agency — the Kyrgyz successor to the Soviet KGB — had grown vastly in influence, becoming the country’s most privileged and influential state body. The new kindergarten, opened in 2024 for staff members’ children, was part of a wave of GKNB construction projects that now dot every region.

And the construction spree was only the most visible sign of the agency’s rise. New laws expanded the GKNB’s powers, giving it control over military units, strategic infrastructure, border protection, and even citizenship, while allowing broader use of force, weapons, and the use of false identities.

title: Slim Shady: Smugglers Eye Big Profits Running Weight Loss Drugs into Brazil
content:
It’s barely 4 a.m. on a June morning, and already the streets of Ciudad del Este in Paraguay are filling up with traders hustling to buy and sell everything from socks to home appliances.

The city — which sits at the point where Paraguay, Brazil, and Argentina meet — welcomes more than 100,000 people daily across the Puente de Amistad (Friendship Bridge) from Brazil. 

But the frontier is also a hot spot for drug smuggling, human trafficking, and money laundering. 

And now, the city’s smugglers have found a new cash cow in tirzepatide — the generic name for the active ingredient in the popular weight loss drug Mounjaro. 

In recent months “tirze” — originally developed to treat type 2 diabetes — has become a prized product for criminal groups operating on the border, according to official seizure data, smugglers, pharmaceutical industry officials, and social media records.

Seizures of the drug have skyrocketed. So far in 2026, Brazilian customs reported that it has already confiscated more than ten times the amount of vials seized in 2025. Last year, Brazilian bank Itaú BBA estimated the black market revenue of the tirze trade to be $485 million.
